pig_day.label: National Pig Day
pig_day.intro: A day for one of the cleverest animals on the farm. Pig fans mark it with piggy banks, pig-shaped everything and a visit to the nearest petting zoo.
funFacts: Pigs barely sweat. They wallow in mud to cool off, and the dried layer works as sunscreen against sunburn.
In lab studies pigs learned to move a cursor across a screen with a joystick, a skill otherwise seen in primates.
Piglets recognise their own mother's voice and come running when she grunts to call them for feeding.

banana_cream_pie_day.label: National Banana Cream Pie Day
banana_cream_pie_day.intro: Sliced banana, vanilla custard and a mountain of whipped cream in a pastry shell. A diner classic that never tried to be elegant, only delicious.
funFacts: Botanically the banana is a berry, while the strawberry is not one.
Nearly every dessert banana sold worldwide is a Cavendish, propagated from cuttings, so the plants are near-identical clones.
The banana plant is not a tree but the world's largest herb; its trunk is made of tightly rolled leaf bases.

if_pets_had_thumbs_day.label: If Pets Had Thumbs Day
if_pets_had_thumbs_day.intro: A cheerful thought experiment: what would the cat do with opposable thumbs, and would the fridge ever stay shut again? Celebrated with treats and a little imagination.
funFacts: Cats and dogs walk on their toes, which is why the joint halfway up the back leg is the heel, not the knee.
Raccoons have no opposable thumb either, yet their sensitive front paws can open latches, lids and jars.
The dewclaw on a dog's leg is a leftover first digit; in some breeds it helps grip bones and steady the leg at speed.

grammar_day.label: National Grammar Day
grammar_day.intro: A day for commas, cases and the joy of a sentence that lands. Cheerfully pedantic rather than strict, and the date is a pun: march forth.
funFacts: The day was launched in 2008 by US author Martha Brockenbrough, founder of the Society for the Promotion of Good Grammar.
A missing comma once cost real money: after a 2017 court ruling on a Maine labour law, a dairy paid its drivers five million dollars in 2018.
English has no official language authority, unlike French with the Académie française or German with its Council for Orthography.

cheese_doodle_day.label: National Cheese Doodle Day
cheese_doodle_day.intro: A salute to the puffed corn snack that turns your fingertips orange. Loud, weightless and impossible to eat just one of.
funFacts: Cheese puffs are made by pushing moist cornmeal through a hot extruder; the sudden drop in pressure makes the dough puff up.
The snack was discovered by accident in 1930s Wisconsin, when a machine for grinding animal feed spat out ribbons of puffed corn.
The orange colour usually comes from annatto, a natural dye made from the seeds of the achiote tree.

frozen_food_day.label: National Frozen Food Day
frozen_food_day.intro: A nod to the freezer, the quiet hero of every kitchen. It keeps peas green in January and dinner possible on the worst of days.
funFacts: Clarence Birdseye developed flash freezing in the 1920s after watching people in Labrador freeze fresh fish in the Arctic wind.
US President Ronald Reagan officially proclaimed 6 March 1984 as National Frozen Food Day.
Freezing fast keeps the ice crystals tiny, so cell walls stay intact and the thawed food is far less mushy.

cereal_day.label: National Cereal Day
cereal_day.intro: A day for the bowl that starts most mornings. Flakes, rings, puffs and the eternal question of how long you can wait before it goes soggy.
funFacts: Corn flakes trace back to 1894, when John Harvey Kellogg and his brother Will rolled out grain dough that had been left standing too long.
Shredded wheat is even older: Henry Perky built the first machine for it in the early 1890s.
The first pre-sweetened breakfast cereal, Ranger Joe, went on sale in the US in 1939; before that people sugared their flakes themselves.

peanut_cluster_day.label: National Peanut Cluster Day
peanut_cluster_day.intro: Roasted peanuts drowned in melted chocolate and left to set in little heaps. Three ingredients, no technique required, endlessly moreish.
funFacts: Peanuts are not nuts but legumes, related to peas and beans, and they ripen underground.
It takes roughly 540 peanuts to fill a standard 340-gram jar of peanut butter.
Chocolate has to be tempered, cooled and rewarmed to a set pattern, or the finished clusters turn dull, soft and streaky grey.

meatball_day.label: National Meatball Day
meatball_day.intro: Almost every cuisine on earth has rolled minced meat into a ball and found it good. Today they all get their moment on the plate.
funFacts: Italian polpette, Swedish köttbullar, Turkish köfte and Chinese lion's head meatballs are all versions of the same simple idea.
In 2018 Sweden's official account admitted that köttbullar came from Turkey, brought home by King Charles XII in the 18th century.
The Roman cookbook known as Apicius already lists isicia, spiced balls of minced meat, well over 1,500 years ago.

bagpipe_day.label: International Bagpipe Day
bagpipe_day.intro: A day for the instrument you can hear from three streets away. It celebrates bagpipes everywhere, not just the Scottish ones.
funFacts: The day was started in 2012 by researchers around the Bagpipe Society to highlight bagpipe traditions beyond Scotland.
There are well over a hundred kinds of bagpipe, from the Galician gaita to the Bulgarian gaida and the German Dudelsack.
A bagpipe cannot pause or play quietly: the bag keeps air flowing, so the sound never stops between notes.

johnny_appleseed_day.label: Johnny Appleseed Day
johnny_appleseed_day.intro: A folklore hero with a real biography. The day remembers the barefoot nurseryman who planted apple trees across the young American Midwest.
funFacts: Johnny Appleseed was John Chapman (1774 to 1845), a nurseryman who planted apple nurseries across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois.
His apples were mostly small, sour spitters grown from seed, destined for cider rather than for eating fresh.
Apple seeds never come true to type: every seedling is a new variety, which is why orchards graft their trees instead.

plant_a_flower_day.label: Plant a Flower Day
plant_a_flower_day.intro: Perfectly timed for the start of spring: put one seed, one bulb or one seedling in the ground and wait. A small act with a very cheerful payoff.
funFacts: Young sunflowers follow the sun across the sky each day; once fully grown they usually settle facing east.
During the Dutch tulip mania of the 1630s, single rare bulbs briefly traded for the price of a house.
A common sowing rule of thumb: bury a seed about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide.

open_an_umbrella_indoors_day.label: National Open an Umbrella Indoors Day
open_an_umbrella_indoors_day.intro: A day built to poke a superstition. Open your umbrella inside the house, see that nothing terrible happens, and enjoy the small rebellion.
funFacts: The day was invented in 2003 by American Thomas Knibb, explicitly to test whether the bad luck ever arrives.
Umbrellas are much older than raincoats: parasols shaded rulers in ancient Egypt, Assyria and China thousands of years ago.
The folding pocket umbrella with a telescopic shaft was patented in Germany in 1928 by engineer Hans Haupt.

pi_day.label: Pi Day
pi_day.intro: The nerdiest and tastiest day of the year: 3.14 written as a date. Mathematicians, teachers and bakers all celebrate it with actual pie.
funFacts: The date works only in US notation, where 14 March is written 3/14, matching the first digits of pi.
The first big Pi Day was held in 1988 by physicist Larry Shaw at the Exploratorium science museum in San Francisco.
Computers have calculated pi to over 100 trillion digits, though about 40 digits suffice to measure the observable universe atom-precisely.

world_contact_day.label: World Contact Day
world_contact_day.intro: In 1953 a group of UFO enthusiasts agreed to think the same message at the same moment, hoping someone out there would hear it. The date stuck.
funFacts: The International Flying Saucer Bureau declared the first World Contact Day in March 1953, with members concentrating on an identical text.
The band Klaatu turned it into the song Calling Occupants of Interplanetary Craft in 1976; The Carpenters made it a hit a year later.
Science does it louder: in 1974 the Arecibo message was beamed toward the star cluster M13, about 25,000 light years away.

panda_day.label: National Panda Day
panda_day.intro: A day for the black and white bear that spends most of its life sitting down and chewing. Few animals are so famously, comfortably unbothered.
funFacts: Giant pandas are true bears, yet about 99 percent of their diet is bamboo, digested with the gut of a carnivore.
A newborn panda weighs around 100 grams, roughly one nine-hundredth of its mother's weight.
An enlarged wrist bone gives pandas a sixth finger of sorts, perfect for gripping bamboo stalks.

corned_beef_and_cabbage_day.label: National Corned Beef and Cabbage Day
corned_beef_and_cabbage_day.intro: Salt-cured beef simmered slowly with cabbage and potatoes. A hearty, unfussy plate that became the signature dish of Irish America.
funFacts: Corned has nothing to do with maize: it refers to the coarse grains, or corns, of salt used to cure the beef.
The pink colour survives cooking because of curing salt containing nitrite, not because the meat is underdone.
In Ireland the classic is bacon and cabbage; beef took over in US cities because it was cheaper there than pork.

sloppy_joe_day.label: National Sloppy Joe Day
sloppy_joe_day.intro: Loose minced beef in tomato sauce, piled on a soft bun and guaranteed to fall apart halfway through. The mess is the entire point.
funFacts: The sandwich takes its name from its behaviour: it is meant to be eaten with a napkin already in hand.
One origin story credits a cook named Joe in Sioux City in the 1930s, another a Havana bar called Sloppy Joe's.
In New Jersey a sloppy joe means something entirely different: a cold triple-decker deli sandwich with rye bread and coleslaw.

lets_laugh_day.label: Let's Laugh Day
lets_laugh_day.intro: A day with one instruction: laugh, and let someone else laugh with you. Cheap, contagious and good for the mood of everyone in the room.
funFacts: Laughter really is contagious: hearing it activates brain areas that prepare your own face to join in.
Rats let out high-pitched 50-kilohertz chirps when tickled, far above what human ears can pick up.
People laugh many times more often in company than alone, which makes laughter mostly a social signal, not a reaction to jokes.

world_frog_day.label: World Frog Day
world_frog_day.intro: Croaking, hopping, staring: frogs are the most conspicuous residents of any pond. World Frog Day is a reminder of how varied — and how endangered — they are.
funFacts: More than 7,700 frog species have been described worldwide, and new ones turn up every year.
The goliath frog of Cameroon grows up to 32 centimetres long and weighs more than three kilograms.
Frogs pull their eyes down into the skull when they swallow, pushing the meal down the throat.

world_puppetry_day.label: World Puppetry Day
world_puppetry_day.intro: Strings, rods, hands and shadows: a day for the oldest kind of theatre, where wood and cloth get to say what people would rather not.
funFacts: The day was proposed in 2000 by Iranian puppeteer Javad Zolfaghari and first celebrated by the puppetry association UNIMA in 2003.
Japanese bunraku puppets are worked by three puppeteers at once, and the lead performer appears with an uncovered face.
Indonesian wayang kulit shadow plays can last all night, with a single dalang voicing every character and cueing the orchestra.

goof_off_day.label: National Goof Off Day
goof_off_day.intro: Officially sanctioned time wasting. Skip the to-do list for a few hours and do something gloriously pointless instead, with a clear conscience.
funFacts: The day is credited to Davis Wallace of Charleston, West Virginia, who proposed it in 1976.
Short breaks genuinely work: studies find brief pauses restore attention better than pushing through a long task.
An idle brain is anything but idle. The default mode network becomes more active as soon as we let our thoughts wander.

puppy_day.label: National Puppy Day
puppy_day.intro: A day for oversized paws, chewed shoes and complete lack of coordination. It also nudges people toward adopting rather than buying.
funFacts: The day was founded in 2006 by American pet advocate Colleen Paige.
Puppies are born deaf and blind; their ear canals open at roughly two to three weeks old.
The pattern of ridges on a dog's nose is as individual as a human fingerprint.

cheesesteak_day.label: National Cheesesteak Day
cheesesteak_day.intro: Thin-sliced beef, griddled onions and melted cheese crammed into a long roll. Philadelphia's most argued-about sandwich gets its own date.
funFacts: The cheesesteak was born in 1930s Philadelphia when hot dog vendor Pat Olivieri grilled beef and put it on his roll.
There is an ordering shorthand at the counter: wiz wit means cheese sauce with fried onions, wiz witout leaves the onions off.
The roll matters as much as the filling: it has to stay soft inside yet firm enough to survive all the juices.

waffle_day.label: International Waffle Day
waffle_day.intro: Scandinavia's sweetest linguistic accident: a church feast day misheard as waffle day. Now it means heart-shaped waffles with jam and cream.
funFacts: The Swedish name Vaffeldagen grew out of Varfrudagen, Our Lady's Day, because the two words sound almost identical.
Medieval waffle irons were often forged with coats of arms or religious scenes, so the pattern was pressed into the batter.
Belgian waffles became a worldwide hit after being sold to visitors at the 1964 New York World's Fair.

spinach_day.label: National Spinach Day
spinach_day.intro: A day for the leaf that shrinks to nothing in the pan and still divides households. Sweet raw, earthy cooked, and unfairly mythologised.
funFacts: Spinach is not an iron powerhouse; even the famous story about a misplaced decimal point turned out to be a legend itself.
Popeye first appeared in 1929 and made spinach a symbol of strength; the town of Crystal City, Texas, erected a Popeye statue in 1937.
Oxalic acid in spinach binds part of its iron and calcium, so the body absorbs less than the nutrition table suggests.

world_theatre_day.label: World Theatre Day
world_theatre_day.intro: A day for the stage in all its forms, from village hall to national theatre. Every year a theatre figure writes a message read around the world.
funFacts: The International Theatre Institute has marked the day since 1962; Jean Cocteau wrote the very first international message.
Wishing luck is taboo backstage: English stages say break a leg, German ones toi toi toi.
The ancient theatre of Epidaurus seats around 14,000 people, and its acoustics carry a whisper to the topmost row.

weed_appreciation_day.label: Weed Appreciation Day
weed_appreciation_day.intro: One day a year the dandelion in the pavement crack gets credit instead of a trowel. Weeds are tough, useful and often edible.
funFacts: Weed is not a botanical category at all. It simply means a plant growing where someone did not want it.
Dandelion, nettle and chickweed are all edible and were kitchen staples long before they were classed as nuisances.
Many weed seeds survive for decades in the soil, waiting for the moment someone turns the earth over.

smoke_and_mirrors_day.label: Smoke and Mirrors Day
smoke_and_mirrors_day.intro: A day for illusion and the pleasure of being fooled on purpose. It is a reminder that things are rarely what they first appear to be.
funFacts: The phrase comes from 18th-century phantasmagoria shows, where ghosts were projected onto clouds of smoke and panes of glass.
The Pepper's ghost illusion, presented in London in 1862, uses one angled sheet of glass and still drives stage and theme park effects.
Magic works on attention: when we focus hard on one thing we can miss something obvious, an effect called inattentional blindness.

pencil_day.label: National Pencil Day
pencil_day.intro: The date of a small but famous patent: the pencil with an eraser stuck on the end. A tool so ordinary that it is easy to forget how clever it is.
funFacts: On 30 March 1858 Hymen Lipman received a US patent for a pencil with a piece of rubber set into its end.
The patent did not survive: in 1875 the US Supreme Court ruled that combining two known objects was not an invention.
Pencil lead has never contained lead. It is graphite mixed with clay, a recipe worked out around 1795.

crayon_day.label: National Crayon Day
crayon_day.intro: A day for the first drawing tool most of us ever held. Crayons are blunt, waxy and still unbeatable for filling a page with colour.
funFacts: Wax crayons are made from paraffin wax and pigment, poured hot into moulds and cooled until solid.
A Yale study ranked the smell of crayons among the twenty most recognisable scents for American adults.
Crayon colour names change with the times: Prussian blue was renamed midnight blue in 1958 because children no longer knew the reference.
